question: m12
q: Is electricity inflation running ahead of overall inflation?

transcript.answer:
**Yes, by a wide margin.** In the year to **August 2026**, electricity prices rose **13.2%**, while overall inflation (all-groups CPI) was **4.0%**. That makes electricity inflation more than three times the headline rate (ABS monthly CPI, Australia, original series).

**How it has moved (annual % change):**

| Month | Electricity | All groups CPI |
|---|---|---|
| Jun 2025 | −6.3 | 1.9 |
| Jul 2025 | 13.6 | 3.0 |
| Oct 2025 | 37.1 | 3.8 |
| Feb 2026 | 37.0 | 3.7 |
| Mar 2026 | 25.4 | 4.6 |
| Jun 2026 | 22.4 | 3.8 |
| Jul 2026 | 6.1 | 3.5 |
| Aug 2026 | 13.2 | 4.0 |

**What the numbers show:**
- **Electricity has been ahead every month since July 2025.** It peaked at about 37% in October 2025 and again in February 2026.
- **The gap has narrowed a lot.** Electricity inflation fell to 6.1% in July 2026, then rose again to 13.2% in August.
- **It was the other way round before mid-2025.** From January to June 2025, electricity prices were falling year on year (−5.9% to −13.2%), while overall inflation was about 2–2.4%.

**Why the swings are so big:** These are year-on-year figures, so they partly reflect the timing of government energy bill rebates. Rebates cut measured power bills in the first half of 2025, and as they were scaled back and ended, the annual rate jumped. So some of the 2025–26 surge is a rebound from an artificially low starting point rather than purely underlying price growth. I haven't checked the exact rebate dates against the data here.

**Why it matters:** Electricity is a fairly small part of the CPI basket, but at these rates it has been adding noticeably to headline inflation. Headline inflation has been around 3.5–4.6% through 2026, above the RBA's 2–3% target band.
